When that happens to multiple motors at once, each one compensates by drawing more current, running hotter, and stressing its winding insulation further. In a food processing facility — with refrigeration compressors, conveyor drives, and processing motors all running in coordination — that clustered sag behavior is a recurring reliability risk, not a background nuisance. Now move to the reactive and harmonic picture. Your average reactive load is 298.8 kVAR — a persistent baseline that never fully clears, even during off-shift valleys. But the dataset maximum is 1,875.2 kVAR. That's the number driving your voltage sags, your transformer thermal burden, and your utility reactive charges. During specific load transitions, your power factor collapses to 69.81% — meaning in those moments, nearly 30% of your apparent power is reactive overhead producing nothing useful. Harmonics are a secondary but continuous condition. Your average iTHD of 5.1%, peaking at 10.2% during drive-intensive moments, is consistent with variable-frequency drives, compressor staging, and conveyor load cycling. At these levels, harmonics add supplementary heat to transformer windings and create potential resonance risk if power factor correction is installed without detuning reactors — something engineering must address in the MPTS design. The financial picture ties all of this together. Direct energy waste is approximately $9,823 per month — about $119,522 per year. Your thermal burden of 251,363 BTU per hour is generating approximately $64,823 annually in active cooling costs alone. Total annual waste, combining reactive losses, thermal burden, and cooling overhead, is approximately $193,550. The correction solution is five H490 MPTS units — 2,000 kVAR of combined reactive compensation capacity, sized from the kVAR MAX of 1,875.2 divided by 400, rounded up to five units. Planning-level installed investment is approximately $1,000,000. Post-correction, this field is projected to reach 99.5% power factor. The voltage sag mechanism is interrupted at its source — reactive surges that currently express as voltage drops are absorbed by the correction bank before they can propagate. Transformer thermal burden drops proportionally with reactive current reduction. The estimated planning-level payback horizon is approximately 5 years on a circuit operating at this utilization level. Before final installation design, I'd recommend four specific engineering confirmations: a reactive surge root cause investigation to time-stamp the 1,875.2 kVAR events against your production schedule; a harmonic filtering assessment to determine whether detuning reactors are required alongside the MPTS bank; a thermal imaging survey of the transformer and upstream bus connections to quantify current hot-spot severity; and interval-level power factor monitoring at or below one-minute resolution during peak shifts to precisely map the 69.81% minimum power factor events. Deli G is a clear candidate for MPTS correction. The field is active, the waste is quantified, and the path to recovery is well-defined. That's electromagnetic stewardship — and that's the Unity standard. ---

**DELIG — Voltage Health | April 2026**

The voltage field for Deli G is telling you something important: this circuit is mechanically healthy enough to sustain production, but it is showing repeated stress events that, left unaddressed, will accumulate into equipment fatigue and eventual reliability failures.

The operational voltage band runs predominantly between 480V and 498.3V — a reasonable range for a 480V nominal system under most conditions. But three annotated voltage dip events stand out clearly. The most severe is 458.2V, occurring near the late-month window around April 26–29. Two additional excursions reached 460.7V and 460.0V respectively, concentrated in the mid-month period around April 14. Each of these represents a voltage sag of 20–22 volts below the 480V nominal — roughly a 4.2 to 4.6% sag.

That percentage may sound small, but in a food processing environment running refrigeration compressors, conveyor drives, and induction motors, a 4–5% voltage sag that repeats and clusters is a meaningful threat. Motor torque falls with the square of voltage — so even a 5% sag can reduce available torque by nearly 10%. When those sags cluster during shift start-up sequences or mid-cycle compressor surges, multiple motors are simultaneously torque-starved, running hotter, and pulling higher current to compensate.

The triangular drop patterns are recurring and grouped — not random noise. The clustering behavior, particularly in the mid-month and late-month windows, is consistent with coordinated motor starts or compressor cycling events that are pulling the field down together. The minimum recorded operational voltage of 458.2V, combined with the clustering frequency, places this circuit in the moderate-to-high device health risk category. Insulation fatigue, nuisance trip risk, and reduced drive electronics lifespan are all elevated under these conditions.
